newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Relief for Russian-American space crew delayed.
newsitem.headline: Relief for Russian-American space crew delayed.

text.p: Stuck in space with toilets close to overflowing, the three-man Russian-American crew of the Mir space station had another blow when they learned that money troubles would delay the departure of their relief crew.
Itar-Tass news agency quoted officials at mission control outside Moscow on Thursday as saying the departure of two Russians and a German scheduled for December 15 had been put back to February.
It said the postponement was caused by financial problems which had delayed production of the Soyuz booster rockets needed for such launches, meaning none was available.

German astronaut Reinhold Ewald had been due to travel with Russians Alexander Lazutkin and Vasily Tsibliyev to replace two Russians and an American on Mir. The current crew now faces a longer stay in space than expected.
"Ewald will not yet achieve his dream of celebrating Christmas and New Year in space," Tass said.
Russian space officials could not be reached for comment.

A delay in the current crew's return to earth had appeared likely after the launch of an unmanned craft which should have brought food, water and fuel to Mir was put off last month because of the cash crisis.

U.S. astronaut John Blaha and his two Russian colleagues, Valery Korzun and Alexander Koleri, have been on board the 10-year-old Mir since September 19. Tass did not set a date for their return to earth.

The last crew on Mir, which included U.S. astronaut Shannon Lucid, stayed longer than planned, partly because of rocket problems. Lucid set endurance records for both Americans and women in space. Another crew, which left Mir last February was forced to stay aboard an extra 52 days.

Making matters worse on Mir is a problem with disposal of bodily waste fluids. Interfax news agency said a device which recycles the crew's waste into the craft's cooling system had broken down and all the reserve containers were nearly full.
Replacements were not due for weeks and the crew could also not find the pump used to transfer the waste into the cooling system, the agency quoted an unidentified source as saying.
New waste containers were to have been shipped out in October but the supply ship was now due to be launched only on November 20.
The problems are the latest to hit Russia's space programme since the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991.

Space agency officials have said their funding is down to about a fifth of Cold War levels. Tass said financial problems had meant a 10-fold cutback in production of Soyuz booster rockets compared with the 1980s.
The Baikonur cosmodrome, from where cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin blasted off in 1961 to become the first man in space, has been deprived of much of its funding.
Moscow also has to pay $115 million a year rent for the base, in the now independent state of Kazakhstan.
On a brighter note, Tass said in a separate report that a Proton booster rocket which is due to deliver an international space probe to Mars was expected to take off as scheduled on November 16.

The Mars probe, which Tass said had funding from 22 countries, will deploy two drilling devices to collect data from the planet. The project has been revived after the cash crisis forced its postponement in 1994.
